sources: University of Minnesota Extension, Carpenter ants: they do not eat wood, they remove it to make galleries for nesting; coarse sawdust near a nest is a sign; indoor nests are usually in moist or decayed wood around tubs, sinks, dishwashers and roofs; workers about 3/8-1/2 inch, queens about 1 inch; parent colonies often outdoors with satellite nests indoors; workers forage mainly sunset to midnight; eat insects, honeydew, meats and sweets; many winged ants indoors in late winter-spring suggest a nest inside, a few winged queens may only be seeking a nest site; find and destroy the nest, replace damaged wood, fix moisture; https://extension.umn.edu/insects-infest-homes/carpenter-ants

University of Maryland Extension, Ants and Termites: How to Tell the Difference: ants have elbowed antennae, termites straight beaded ones; ants have a pinched waist, termites do not; ant front wings are longer than hind wings, termite wings are about equal in length; https://extension.umd.edu/resource/ants-and-termites-how-tell-difference

beats.say: Giant black ants are chewing tunnels through the wood in your walls.
And the queen can be an inch long.
Carpenter ants. The workers, half an inch long.
They don't even eat the wood. They chew it out, to make room for the nest.
The clue? Little piles of coarse sawdust.
They come out to hunt at night, from sunset to midnight.
And the big nest is often outside. The one in your walls is just a second home.
